articles.body: The precedent of US involvement in Vietnam started with President Truman’s decision in 1950 to provide the French with $23 million for the war effort in Indochina, driven by communism’s rise in China and the Korean War, which began the integral logic Gelb and Betts call “strategic linkage”, whereby each concession by the now dominant US was construed as a falling domino in a fragile world order.  This logic subsequently became publicly known policy in 1954, when Eisenhower explained the reasoning of US interest in Indochina: “You have a row of dominoes set up, you knock over the first one, and what will happen to the last one is the certainty that it will go over very quickly.”  Eisenhower’s push to limit the spread of communism in the region was the first construction of a framework that Johnson relied on as justification a decade later. This precise and public establishment of policy was almost verbatim what Johnson later invoked, with such continuity indicating Johnson’s reliance on his predecessors’ foreign policy initiatives. Between 1954 and 1960, Eisenhower had pledged material support to Diem’s government and stationed 685 military advisers in South Vietnam. Hess sees the cumulative power of three presidents pledging to defend the country as creating a ‘vital interest’, which left the ‘prestige and credibility’ of the US resting on the survival of South Vietnam.  NSAM 273 is the clearest piece of primary evidence suggesting the war was an inheritance for Lyndon Johnson. It opens by stating, ‘it remains the central object of the United States in South Vietnam to assist the people…to win their contest’, language that indisputably reaffirms Kennedy-era policy.  The first draft of this memorandum was in fact written by McGeorge Bundy – an advisor Johnson inherited from Kennedy and chose to keep until 1966 – before the assassination of Kennedy, suggesting that the language was inherited and Johnson simply fulfilled the legacy of his deceased predecessor.  One ought to additionally recognise that the structural weight of this commitment was material, not simply rhetorical: by the time Lyndon Johnson was sworn in, the US had 16,732 military personnel in Vietnam and had committed billions in aid.
